raw_response:
I'm 57 years old and I've been farming these 5.5 mu for 35 years. My husband and I do most of the work ourselves — our son and daughter-in-law work in the county town at a factory, so they send money home but aren't here for the busy seasons except maybe at harvest. Five and a half mu isn't much, but it's what we have, and every jiao counts.

This year I'm planting winter wheat on all 5.5 mu, same as always. Last year the wheat gave me about 420 jin per mu, which was decent — not great, not bad. The extension fellow who came by last spring said I could try a new high-yield variety, but the seed costs more and honestly, I've been using this Jinmai 47 for years, it knows my land and I know it. I'll stick with improved seed, not the fanciest hybrid, but good reliable stock. I buy fresh seed every couple of years, this year I saved some from last year but it didn't germinate so well, so I'm buying new. That'll cost me about 35 yuan per mu.

For fertilizer, last year I put down 50 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as base, and topdressed with urea at jointing. The wheat looked a bit yellow early on, so this year I'll do about the same — maybe a touch more base fertilizer. I'm thinking 20 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) per mu at planting, then if the wheat looks strong at green-up, I'll topdress with 10 kg urea per mu. That's about 18 kg of nitrogen total per mu, which is what I usually do. The soil here is alright, not the best, not the worst. I can't afford to throw money at it — my son's factory job helps but we still need cash for daily expenses.

Irrigation is the big cost. Water from the well isn't free anymore — they meter it now, and pumping costs electricity. For wheat, I usually irrigate three times: once at planting if it's dry, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. If winter snow is good I might skip the early one. For the maize I'll plant after wheat harvest, I'll irrigate once or twice depending on the summer rains. Last July was so dry I had to pump twice and it hurt. I'm budgeting for two irrigations on maize.

Speaking of the maize — I'll plant it in mid-June right after the wheat comes off. There's no time to waste, maybe a week at most. I usually hire Wang's tractor to do a quick till and then plant. For maize seed, I use hybrid, about 2 kg per mu, costs around 40 yuan per mu. Fertilizer for maize: I put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 15 kg per mu, and if the summer rains come good and the crop looks promising, I might topdress with a little urea at the big喇叭口 stage. Maybe 15 kg N per mu total for maize.

Pesticides — I use herbicide on both crops, it's cheaper than weeding by hand and my back isn't what it used to be. For wheat, I spray for weeds in early spring, and watch for aphids. For maize, I use a pre-emergent herbicide and maybe one insecticide spray if the borers show up. I don't spray unless I see something — at 40 yuan a bottle, I think twice.

Labor: my husband and I do almost everything. At wheat harvest and maize planting, that week is brutal — we might hire two laborers for 3 days each to help with the rush. That's 120 yuan per day now, so I try to keep hired days to a minimum. Family labor is probably 25 days for wheat and 20 days for maize, plus 6 days hired total across both crops.

Yield expectation? If the weather cooperates and I don't get hit with disease, I'm hoping for 450 kg per mu on wheat and 500 kg per mu on maize. That's a bit optimistic maybe, but last year was close on maize. Wheat prices are about 2.4 yuan per jin, maize around 1.2 — if I hit those yields, we'll cover costs and have a little left.

Total input costs? Let me count — seed, fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation, hired labor. I'm guessing around 2,800 yuan total for both crops. I have about 3,500 yuan set aside from my son's remittance, so I should be okay, but there's not much margin. That's why I'm not trying anything new this year — stick with what works, don't lose money.
